The Lantern Keeper

On the northern edge of the marsh there was a stone tower, and in the tower lived a woman named Orla Fenwick, who kept the lantern. Every evening, when the light went grey over the reeds, she climbed the one hundred and twelve steps to the top, trimmed the wick, filled the reservoir with oil, and struck a match. The flame was small at first, a yellow bead no bigger than a thumbnail, but the glass around it had been ground by a clever hand long ago, and it threw the light far across the water, so that the boatmen coming home from the river mouth could find the channel between the mud banks.

Nobody remembered who had built the tower. The miller said it was older than the village, and the village was older than the church, and the church had a bell with a date on it that nobody could read any more. Orla did not much care who had built it. She cared that the steps were sound, that the oil was dry, and that the shutters on the seaward side closed tightly when the wind came hard out of the east.

In the winter of the long frost, the river froze for the first time in forty years. The boats stayed in the harbour, tied up and silent, their ropes stiff with ice. There was no one to guide, and the miller told her she might as well let the lantern go dark until spring. Orla thanked him for his advice and climbed the steps that evening as she always did.

It was on the ninth night of the frost that she saw the other light. It was far out on the marsh, low down, where no house had ever stood. It flickered and went out, and then it came back, a little nearer. She watched it for an hour, and in that hour it moved slowly toward the tower, stopping now and then, as if whoever carried it was unsure of the way.

She went down the steps, put on her heavy coat and her boots, and took the hand lamp from its hook by the door. The cold struck her face like a slap. The reeds were stiff and white, and the ice between them was thick enough to walk on, though it groaned under her feet. She called out, and her voice went flat and small across the marsh.

An answer came back, thin and tired. She followed it, holding the lamp high, until she found a boy sitting on a hummock of frozen grass with a candle in a tin cup. He was perhaps eleven years old, and he had been walking since the morning. His name, he said, was Tobias, and he had come from the farms on the far side of the river, because his grandmother was ill and his mother had sent him for the doctor, and the doctor lived in the village, and the bridge was broken, and he had thought the ice would carry him across.

The ice had carried him, but the marsh had turned him round and round, and every path had looked the same, until he had seen the lantern on the tower and set his course by it. Then his candle had blown out, and he had lost his nerve, and sat down.

Orla brought him to the tower and gave him bread and hot milk by the stove. Then she woke the doctor, who grumbled and found his bag and his boots. In the grey before dawn the three of them crossed the ice together, the doctor in front with a long pole to test the way, Orla behind with the lamp, and the boy between them, pointing toward the farms.

The grandmother lived. She lived another eleven years, in fact, and told the story at every wedding and every funeral, and each time it grew a little, until the lantern was brighter than the sun and the boy had crossed the marsh through a blizzard with wolves at his heels. Tobias, who had grown tall and quiet, never corrected her.

When the river thawed, the boats came back, and the boatmen once more steered by the light from the tower. Orla went on climbing the one hundred and twelve steps every evening. The miller stopped telling her to let the lantern go dark. And on the tenth night of every winter, whether the river froze or not, a young man came across from the far side with a basket of eggs and a jar of honey, and sat with her by the stove, and they did not talk very much, because there was no need to.

Years later, when her knees could no longer manage the steps, it was Tobias who climbed them for her. He trimmed the wick and filled the reservoir with oil and struck the match, and the small yellow flame grew bright behind the old ground glass, and threw its light across the water as it always had, for anyone who might be out there in the dark, looking for the way home.
